snapshot.title: SSC English: Sentence Improvement & Cloze Test
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ SSC English Hook: Each: Singular. Besides: Extra. Beside: Next. If had: Would have. SON rule. Cloze: Flow first.

quick_notes.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
quick_notes.detail: Singular sub : Singular verb. (e.g., "Each of the boys IS"). "Neither...nor" takes verb according to second subject.
quick_notes.explanation: Subject-verb agreement means that the subject of a sentence and its verb must match in number: a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. For example, in the sentence "Each of the boys is here," the subject is "each" which is singular, so the verb is "is" not "are." When using the correlative conjunction "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the subject that is closest to it, meaning the second subject after "nor" determines whether the verb is singular or plural. For instance, in "Neither the teacher nor the students are ready," the verb "are" is plural because "students" is plural, but in "Neither the students nor the teacher is ready," the verb "is" is singular because "teacher" is singular.

quick_notes.title: Confusing Words
quick_notes.detail: Beside (By the side of), whereas Besides (In addition to). Affect (Verb), whereas Effect (Noun). Lose, whereas Loose.
quick_notes.explanation: Beside means "by the side of," as in "The book is beside the lamp," while besides means "in addition to," as in "Besides the book, there is a pen." Affect is a verb meaning "to influence," for example "The weather affects my mood," whereas effect is a noun meaning "a result," like "The effect of the rain was flooding." Lose means "to misplace or fail to win," such as "I lose my keys often," and loose means "not tight or free," as in "The screw is loose."

quick_notes.title: Cloze Test Strategy
quick_notes.detail: 1. Read the whole passage first. 2. Understand the tone (Positive/Negative). 3. Look for clues in the next sentence. 4. Check for fixed collocations.
quick_notes.explanation: A cloze test is a type of exercise where some words are removed from a passage, and you must choose the correct word to fill each blank. First, read the entire passage from start to finish to understand its overall meaning, which helps you see how each blank fits into the story or argument. Next, decide whether the passage has a positive tone, meaning it uses happy or approving words, or a negative tone, meaning it uses sad or disapproving words, because the word you choose must match that feeling. Then, look at the sentence right after the blank for clues, such as a word like "however" or "therefore," which tells you if the blank should show a contrast or a result. Finally, check for fixed collocations, which are word pairs that always go together, like "make a decision" or "heavy rain," because the correct word often forms a common phrase with the words around it.

quick_notes.title: Conditional Sentences
quick_notes.detail: 1. If + Present, Will + V1. 2. If + Past, Would + V1. 3. If + Past Perfect, Would have + V3. (SSC Favorite).
quick_notes.explanation: Conditional sentences are used to talk about situations that depend on something else happening. There are three main types. The first type is for real and possible future situations: you use "if" with a present tense verb, and the other part of the sentence uses "will" plus the base form of the verb, for example, "If it rains, I will take an umbrella." The second type is for unreal or imaginary situations in the present or future: you use "if" with a past tense verb, and the other part uses "would" plus the base verb, like "If I had a million dollars, I would travel the world." The third type is for unreal situations in the past, meaning something did not happen: you use "if" with the past perfect tense (had plus past participle), and the other part uses "would have" plus the past participle, for example, "If I had studied, I would have passed the test."

quick_notes.title: Parallelism
quick_notes.detail: Structure of items in a list should be same. (e.g., "Swimming, dancing and to sing" is WRONG. Use "singing").
quick_notes.explanation: Parallelism is a grammar rule that means all items in a list must have the same grammatical form. For example, if you list activities, each one should be a verb in the same tense or form, like "swimming, dancing, and singing," not a mix like "swimming, dancing, and to sing" because "to sing" is an infinitive while the others are gerunds. To check for parallelism, look at each item in a series and make sure they all use the same type of word or phrase, such as all nouns, all adjectives, or all verbs in the same form. This keeps your writing clear and easy to understand for the reader.
